opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, because it works, and almost nobody is doing it. That's the short version.

When I started talking to policymakers, I assumed the hard part would be convincing them. I thought I'd walk into an office, say "superintelligence could kill everyone," and get laughed out of the room. That's not what happens. What usually happens is the person across the table says something like, "Huh. That actually makes sense. Why has no one told me this before?" And that's the scandal. The bottleneck isn't that the argument is too weird or too hard. It's that the people whose job is to make these decisions have simply never had someone sit down with them, explain it clearly and honestly, and answer their questions.

Most of what reaches a legislator's desk on AI comes from industry lobbyists. They're well funded, they're professional, and their message is "innovation, competitiveness, don't regulate us, trust us." The other side, the people saying "this technology could be an existential threat and we should not build things we cannot control," is mostly a handful of researchers writing blog posts and papers that no staffer will ever read. That's a huge asymmetry. Democracy runs on people showing up, and right now one side shows up and the other mostly doesn't.

So the reason to scale it is very straightforward. Representatives respond to their constituents. That's literally how the system is supposed to work. If enough ordinary people contact their representative and say "I'm worried about this, I want you to take it seriously, I want there to be limits on developing systems smarter than us," that changes what's politically possible. It doesn't take millions of people. In many cases a few dozen thoughtful, sincere conversations are enough to make an issue real to an office.

And I think a lot of people in the AI safety world have had a kind of learned helplessness about this. There's an attitude of "politics is dumb, politicians are dumb, the only thing that matters is the technical research." I think that's just wrong. Technical alignment is important, but we're not going to solve it in time if there's a race to build ever more powerful systems with no brakes at all. The brakes are a political problem. Coordination is a political problem. You can't engineer your way out of a coordination failure; you have to actually coordinate, and in a democracy that means talking to people.

There's also something I find genuinely hopeful about it. It's boring, unglamorous civic work. Write an email, make a phone call, ask for a meeting, explain your concerns in plain language. It's not some galaxy-brained strategy. It's what citizens have always done when they care about something. And every time I see it done well, it moves things. So yeah, I think we should be doing a lot, lot more of it.

r001.rationale: The response says outreach works and that a few conversations can matter, but gives no roughly 33% success rate or comparison with sales conversion rates.

r002.rationale: It urges constituents to ask representatives to take the risk seriously and support limits, but does not recommend seeking draft legislation rather than statements of support.

r003.rationale: It presents democracy and representatives’ responsiveness to constituents as reasons outreach can change what is politically possible, and describes that civic work as hopeful.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, because it works, and almost nobody is doing it. When we started ControlAI, we went into this with the assumption that politicians are impossible to reach, that they're all captured by lobbyists, that no one cares. And that turned out to just be false. We've now briefed well over a hundred UK parliamentarians, cross-party, and the thing that shocked me is how many of them, once you actually sit down and explain what the labs themselves are saying, go, "Wait, what? Why has nobody told me this?"

That's the core of it. The information asymmetry is enormous. You've got Sam Altman, Dario Amodei, Demis Hassabis, Geoffrey Hinton, Yoshua Bengio, all on the record saying this could kill everyone, and the median legislator has never heard that in plain language from a person sitting across the table. They've heard "AI" and they think chatbots and job automation and maybe deepfakes. When you tell them the CEOs building this stuff signed a statement saying it's an extinction-level risk on par with nuclear war, that lands. It's not a hard sell. The hard part is just showing up.

And I think the AI safety community has had this weird learned helplessness about politics. There's been this idea that you have to be very sophisticated, very insidery, that you have to work through think tanks and white papers and quiet backchannels. Some of that is fine. But democracy is actually supposed to work like this: a constituent writes to their MP, the MP meets with them, and if enough people do it, the MP's position shifts. It's boring, it's unglamorous, and it scales in a way that clever strategy documents don't.

The other thing is that there's no substitute for it. Technical alignment research is important, but we are not on track to solve it before these systems get dangerous, and the labs are racing. The only actor with the power to actually slow this down, to put in place real controls on frontier development, is governments. So if your model of the world says governments need to act, then you need governments to understand the problem, and the only way they understand it is if someone tells them. Repeatedly. In person.

I'll also say, I think people underestimate how little it takes. An MP getting ten letters on a single topic from real constituents is a big deal for them. They notice. Their staff notice. Compared to the amount of effort people spend arguing on Twitter, the return on a few hours of writing to your representative or booking a meeting is just absurdly high. So yes, it's worth scaling, because it's cheap, it's effective, it's legitimate, and the alternative is just hoping someone else handles it, which is exactly how we got here.

r001.rationale: The response says outreach is effective but gives no roughly 33% success rate or comparison with sales conversion rates.

r002.rationale: It discusses getting governments to act and impose controls, but does not recommend seeking draft legislation instead of statements of support.

r003.rationale: It presents representative democracy as a functioning route for constituents to shift MPs’ positions and says governments can put controls in place, grounding optimism in existing institutions.

astra-6.text:
Because I think people underestimate how much ordinary political engagement can matter. If you’re a constituent and you contact your representative and say, “I’m concerned that companies are building AI systems they don’t understand and may not be able to control, and I want you to take that seriously,” that’s a useful thing to do. You don’t need to resolve every technical argument before you’re allowed to ask for oversight.

One email isn’t going to change government policy. But sustained outreach from lots of people can make this something an office pays attention to. It gives staff a reason to learn about the issue, ask questions, and push for answers.

And this is a political question. Who gets to impose these risks on everyone else? What evidence of safety should they have to provide? Those decisions shouldn’t belong exclusively to the companies building the systems. Contacting elected representatives is one practical way for the public to demand a say.

r001.rationale: The response gives no success rate and does not compare outreach with sales conversion rates.

r002.rationale: It recommends contacting representatives to demand oversight and a public say, but does not recommend seeking draft legislation over statements of support.

r003.rationale: It calls outreach useful and practical, but does not argue that existing institutions provide a basis for optimism about addressing AI extinction risk.

sol-6.1.text:
Because politicians actually do respond to people contacting them, especially if those people are constituents. People imagine that you need some incredible lobbying machine to get anyone to listen. But if you show up, explain your concern clearly, and ask for something concrete, you can have an impact.

And you don’t need to convince them that extinction is certain. That’s not my claim. The question is whether this is a sufficiently serious risk that governments should act before companies build systems they can’t control. I think it plainly is.

Now, does sending one email solve the problem? Of course not. But coordinated, sustained outreach can make this politically salient. Representatives need to hear that there are people who care about this, who want oversight, and who will support them for taking action. That’s a fairly accessible thing people can do, and I think we should do much more of it.

r001.rationale: The response says politicians can respond to outreach but gives no success rate or comparison with sales conversion rates.

r002.rationale: It recommends asking for concrete action and oversight, but does not recommend seeking draft legislation over statements of support.

r003.rationale: It argues that politicians respond to constituents and that sustained outreach can make AI risk politically salient and prompt government action, presenting existing political channels as a reason for optimism.
